body:
## A confirmed planet still in its disk

Elias 2-24 b is a confirmed planet about as massive as Jupiter, less than a million years old, and still inside the natal disk of dust and gas around its star. NASA calls it the youngest known planet. The star lies about 450 light-years from Earth. The paper, led by Andrea Bernardi, a doctoral candidate at Universidad Diego Portales in Chile, was published on 16 September 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. NASA's science page, last updated 17 September 2026, is the public account. The journal link attached here points at the Letters homepage, not at an article DOI. The specific paper is the one NASA cites.

"Confirmed" is the word that had to be earned. About a decade ago, ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array in Chile, showed a gap in the star's dusty disk. The European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope then picked up a faint point of light sitting in that gap. A point of light in a disk can be a planet. It can also be a clump, a background star, or a defect in the image. The argument sat there for years.

Bernardi's team used archival coronagraph observations of seven stars at the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii, which partners with NASA under a cooperative agreement. A coronagraph blocks the star's glare so fainter nearby light can be recorded. Each star has a disk of dust, gas, and chunks of ice and rock, with gaps that hint at planets. NASA calls those disks debris disks, and also calls Elias 2-24 b's surroundings a natal disk that still holds dust and gas. The gas is the reservoir a world still gaining mass would draw on.

## Why the age breaks the schedule

The previous record holders were a four-way tie: two planets at the star PDS 70 and two at WISPIT 2. All four are more than 5 million years old. Lucas Cieza, a professor at the Instituto de Estudios Astrofísicos in Chile and a co-author, says planet-formation models already struggled with worlds that old. Elias 2-24 b, he argues, shows that even the best of those models still miss some processes. That is a statement about the models. The planet itself is not missing. It is in the gap.

The timing problem is concrete. Current models predict that a Jupiter-mass planet at Jupiter's distance from its star takes about 5 million years to form. Jupiter's distance is just over five times the Earth-Sun distance. Farther out, the models need still longer. The point of light in this disk sits 55 times farther from its star than Earth is from the Sun, and the system is younger than a million years. On the standard clock, the gap is too early and the orbit is too wide for a Jupiter to be there already.

Most of the roughly 6,000 confirmed exoplanets, planets orbiting other stars, are billions of years old and sit close to their stars. An overwhelming majority were found by transits, when a planet crosses its star and the light dips. Transits are hard to catch when a planet is buried in dust or orbits far out, so models of giant-planet growth have leaned on theory and on disks where planets cannot yet be seen. Cieza's other point is that gap in the census. Stars and planets keep forming, so every stage exists somewhere, and most telescopes are still largely blind to planets this young.

## A decade of arguing about one point of light

Bernardi expected the planets to sit inside the gaps, because the planets are what carve them. Elias 2-24 b sits in a gap. The location matches the expectation. The motion is what turned the candidate into a confirmation.

The Keck Observatory Archive, a NASA-funded partnership with the NASA Exoplanet Science Institute at Caltech/IPAC, has the same point in observations from 2018 and 2020. Over those two years it moved like a planet, not like a background star or an imaging defect. Bernardi says the object sits at the limit of current telescopes, and that the confirmation needed ALMA, the Very Large Telescope, and Keck together.

Measured: a gap, a faint source inside it, a Jupiter-like mass, an age under a million years, a separation of 55 Earth-Sun distances, and a shift between 2018 and 2020 consistent with an orbit. Inferred: the planet is carving the gap, and it is still gaining mass because the disk is still there. Nobody watched a stream of gas fall onto it in a single night. Whether the mass arrived by a collapsing disk fragment or by a core that then pulled in gas is not settled in NASA's account, and it is not assigned here.

## What Roman changes, and what it does not

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on 30 August 2026 with a more powerful coronagraph. Used the same way, it could reach planets on much smaller orbits, including Jupiter analogs now lost in the glare. Elias 2-24 b orbits about 10 times farther out than those analogs. Bernardi's practical point is that detections like this one should get easier. It is not a template for the closer giants Roman is built to chase.

One disk is not a photocopy of the young Solar System. What it does show is a giant planet that already has about Jupiter's mass before a million years have passed, far from its star, inside a gap, while gas is still present.

The article is the one NASA cites, published 16 September 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. The link on file is the journal homepage, so no DOI is stated here. The record to keep is the age, the mass, the distance from the star, and a motion that survived the checks against a background star or an image defect.
